entries.claim: Are early strength gains neural or muscular?
entries.locked_value: BOTH, and sooner than the 1988 model claimed: measurable hypertrophy appears earlier than the old dogma said (early 'growth' partly edema/damage, but growth is real sooner)
entries.source: Sale 1988 (old model); Damas et al., J Physiol 2016 (correction of record)
entries.note: Critic 2 · 1.7 — present as nuanced, not as settled 'neural only'

entries.claim: Creatine monohydrate — primary mechanism and dose
entries.locked_value: 3–5 g/day; primary mechanism is phosphocreatine/ATP resynthesis; cell volumization is secondary
entries.note: Critic 2 · 1.8 — never lead with 'cell hydration'

entries.locked_value: LONG holds (>45–60 s) transiently reduce force/power; SHORT holds (<30 s) in a warm-up are trivial
entries.source: Behm et al., Appl Physiol Nutr Metab 2016
entries.note: Critic 2 · 1.10 — 'never stretch before lifting' is itself a bro-myth

entries.claim: How close to failure to train
entries.locked_value: Similar hypertrophy from ~0–3 RIR when effort is equated; leave 1–2 reps in reserve for most sets
entries.source: Refalo et al., Sports Med 2023 (systematic review)
entries.note: Critic 2 · 2.5 — the peer-ring argument; say 'effort-equated' out loud

entries.locked_value: 10–20 hard sets/muscle/week is the practical band; returns rise to a point then flatten — the ceiling is debated
entries.source: Schoenfeld et al. 2017 dose-response; ongoing debate
entries.note: Critic 2 · 2.5 — acknowledge the ceiling debate rather than pretending it's settled

entries.locked_value: Full ROM with load generally wins for hypertrophy; partials at long muscle lengths can be a useful adjunct, not a replacement

entries.claim: How much fluid the heart moves per day
entries.locked_value: cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min ≈ 7,500 L/day; you hold only ~5 L at any moment
entries.source: Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology
entries.note: SHIPPED as EP-06 opener. Frame: the body is a fleet, not a tank.

entries.claim: Heart-rate cost of water loss (EP-06 THE DATUM)
entries.locked_value: ≈ +3 bpm for every 1% of body mass lost as water, at a fixed intensity
entries.source: Adams et al., Sports Med 2014 (systematic review); Montain & Coyle, J Appl Physiol 1992
entries.note: SHIPPED as EP-06. Say 'at the same pace' — the drift is intensity-normalised.

entries.claim: Where the 2% dehydration rule came from
entries.locked_value: the 2% line was set in fixed-intensity lab protocols; in real time-trial conditions dehydration up to ~4% body mass did not impair performance
entries.source: Goulet, Sports Med 2012 (meta-analysis, 28 effect estimates); Cheuvront & Kenefick 2014, Comprehensive Physiology
entries.note: SHIPPED as EP-06 honesty beat. This correction IS the brand — ship it against our own genre.

entries.claim: Overdrinking water can be fatal (exercise-associated hyponatraemia)
entries.locked_value: ≥14 athlete deaths since 1981; the 2015 consensus's prevention advice is: drink to thirst, not to a number
entries.source: Hew-Butler et al., Clin J Sport Med 2015 (3rd International EAH Consensus; also BJSM 49:1432)
entries.note: SHIPPED as EP-06. Never pair with a hydration-volume CTA. Rate factor: exercise duration >4 h, readily available fluids.

entries.locked_value: no scientific basis for healthy adults; the advice traces to a 1945 US Food & Nutrition Board line whose next sentence says most of the day's water comes from food
entries.source: Valtin, Am J Physiol 2002 (invited review); Negoianu & Goldfarb, JASN 2008
entries.note: SHIPPED as EP-06. Exceptions: kidney stones, hot/humid conditions, strenuous work — say them if the topic needs it.

entries.claim: The kidney's daily workload and return
entries.locked_value: ≈180 L filtered per day (GFR ≈ 125 mL/min); ~99% returned to the blood
entries.source: Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology
entries.note: SHIPPED as EP-06 proof beat. Textbook figure — keep the word 'about'.

entries.claim: How to replace what you lose
entries.locked_value: weigh before/after (1 kg lost ≈ 1 L); replace 1.2–1.5 × the loss over the next few hours; keep losses ≤2% (≈1.4 kg at 70 kg)
entries.source: ACSM position stand; 2015 EAH consensus (drink to thirst)
entries.note: SHIPPED as EP-06 protocol. The 1.2–1.5 factor exists because urine keeps being made.

entries.locked_value: not proven; across a 161 km ultramarathon, blood sodium did not separate crampers from non-crampers
entries.source: Hoffman & Stuempfle, Sports Med Open 2015 (also 'Sodium intake during an ultramarathon does not prevent cramping', 2015)
entries.note: SHIPPED as EP-06 receipt. Fix fluid, load, sleep and pacing first; sodium is a maybe.

entries.locked_value: in mice, interstitial space expands ~60% in sleep and CSF/Aβ clearance roughly doubles
entries.source: Xie/Nedergaard, Science 2013; Iliff 2012, Sci Transl Med
entries.note: RESERVE for a sleep episode — must carry 'in mice' on the card. Not shipped in EP-06.

entries.claim: Why the scale jumps after a carb day
entries.locked_value: each gram of muscle glycogen is stored with ~3 g (up to 17 g when fully rehydrated) of water
entries.source: Fernández-Elías et al., Eur J Appl Physiol 2015
entries.note: RESERVE for the scale topic. The 1:17 figure is a single trial — bound it.

entries.claim: Relative hypertrophy response to the same resistance-training programme
entries.locked_value: Across 10 studies, males and females had no significant difference in relative hypertrophy response to the same programme.
entries.source: Roberts, Nuckols & Krieger, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2020; systematic review and meta-analysis; 12 hypertrophy outcomes from 10 studies, ES 0.07 ± 0.06, p=0.31.
entries.note: This does not say women cannot build muscle. It says resistance training can build muscle in both sexes; “bulky” is not an accidental one-session outcome.

entries.claim: Resistance training outcomes in healthy adult women
entries.locked_value: Resistance training improved strength and produced a moderate hypertrophy effect in the female-only synthesis; training duration in included studies ranged from 4 weeks to 12 months.
entries.source: Hagstrom et al., Sports Medicine, 2020; systematic review and meta-analysis; 24 studies, 15 hypertrophy outcomes; DOI 10.1007/s40279-019-01247-x.
entries.note: Use to state that muscle change is a gradual adaptation measured over weeks to months. Do not promise an individual result.
